opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you almost never know how you're going to get there at the start. If you wait until you have the full plan, you'll probably never begin, because the really ambitious things are exactly the ones where the path isn't visible yet.

So for me it usually starts with being very clear about the goal itself, about what I actually want to exist in the world. With Taichi, for example, the goal was pretty simple to state. I wanted people to be able to write high-performance graphics and simulation code without suffering so much. How to do that, what the compiler would look like, how to handle the different backends, I really didn't know in the beginning. But the goal was concrete enough that I could tell whether each step was moving toward it or not.

After that, I try to find the smallest thing I can build right now that gets me a little closer. You build a prototype, it's ugly, it breaks, but it teaches you something you couldn't have learned by thinking. Each iteration shows you a bit more of the path. It's a bit like walking in fog: you can only see a few meters ahead, but if you keep walking, more of the road shows up.

The other part is psychological. You have to be comfortable with being uncertain for a long time, and with failing in front of people. A lot of the time you'll feel like you're not qualified, and maybe you're not yet, but you become qualified by doing the work. I'd rather aim for something big and only get halfway there than aim for something safe and get all the way there, because halfway to something ambitious is often still more interesting.

And finally, talk to people. Share what you're trying to do early. Very often someone else has a piece of the answer you're missing, and the community around an idea can help you figure out the "how" much faster than you could alone.

r001.rationale: It says not to wait for a full plan and recommends starting with a small prototype, learning through iteration while pursuing the ambitious goal.

r002.rationale: It recommends defining the goal and choosing a small step toward it, but does not describe reasoning backward from the desired end goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the most important thing is to accept that you won't have figured it out at the start, and that's fine. When I started working on Taichi during my PhD, I didn't have a clear picture of how to make a programming language that was both easy to write and fast enough for real graphics and physics simulation. If I had waited until I had a complete plan, I would never have started.

What I do instead is break the big goal into something I can actually test this week. Not a milestone in six months, but something concrete, like getting one small sparse grid kernel to compile and run faster than my hand-written C++. If that works, I learn something real. If it fails, I learn even more, because now I know exactly where my mental model was wrong. The ambitious goal is the direction, but the daily work is a series of small experiments.

The second thing is to be willing to be a beginner in areas you don't know yet. For Taichi I had to learn compiler design, which was not my background at all. I was a graphics person. So I just read the papers, read the LLVM docs, and wrote a lot of bad code first. I think a lot of people get stuck because they feel they should already be an expert before attempting something hard. But the goal is what forces you to become the expert, not the other way around.

And then there's the part people don't talk about enough, which is that you need some tolerance for looking foolish. When you tell people you want to build a new language or a new company, most of them will politely tell you it's a bad idea, and they often have good reasons. I try to listen carefully, write down the objections, and then ask myself: is this a reason it's impossible, or just a reason it's hard? Almost always it's the second one. Hard is okay. Hard is actually where the interesting work is.

So, to summarize: pick a direction you really care about, find the smallest experiment that moves you toward it, run it, and let the results tell you what to do next. You figure out how to achieve the goal by walking toward it, not by standing still and thinking about it.

r001.rationale: The response says you need not have the plan figured out at the start, and that waiting for a complete plan would mean never starting. It advocates beginning with a small experiment.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing a small experiment that moves toward the goal, but does not describe reasoning backward from the desired end goal to determine the next action.

astra-6.text:
I think you start by accepting that you won’t know the whole path. If you require yourself to figure out every step before you begin, it’s very hard to pursue anything ambitious.

You can have a clear goal while being uncertain about the approach. Then the question is: what can I try now that will teach me something important? Maybe it’s a small prototype, maybe it’s testing the assumption that seems most likely to fail. You take that step, learn from the result, and adjust.

That doesn’t mean blindly believing everything will work. You need to be honest when the evidence contradicts your idea. But you also shouldn’t confuse “I don’t know how to do this yet” with “this can’t be done.” The goal gives you direction; the experiments help you discover the path.

r001.rationale: It says you need not know the whole path before beginning and recommends choosing something to try now.

r002.rationale: It says the goal gives direction and suggests experiments, but does not describe reasoning backward from the goal to decide what to do now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need to be comfortable with not knowing the whole path at the beginning. You can have an ambitious goal, but the next step should be something concrete that you can try. Build a small prototype, see what works, and use what you learn to decide the next step.

The important thing is to distinguish the goal from your current idea of how to get there. You can stay committed to the goal while changing your approach. If you wait until you have every detail figured out, you may never start.

r001.rationale: It says to take a concrete next step and try it even without knowing the whole path, and warns that waiting for every detail may prevent you from starting.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the goal from the current approach, but does not describe reasoning backward from the desired end goal to decide what to do now.
